cmds.n: Every commit that touched the file; click one to read that version. In Blame view, the stacked-rectangles icon beside a hunk re-blames before that change, walking attribution backward layer by layer.

intents.q: Search commit messages across GitHub

cmds.n: Commit-message search, scoped by repo, org, or author. On the site, pick Commits in the search result tabs.

intents.q: Follow releases without a GitHub account

cmds.n: A feed any RSS reader takes. tags.atom and commits/<branch>.atom exist too. With an account, Watch -> Custom -> Releases does the same through notifications.

intents.q: Stop typing the same review comment

cmds.n: Reusable comment snippets, inserted from the toolbar icon or Ctrl+. in any comment box. The kind welcome for first-time contributors writes itself once.

intents.q: Git's move beyond SHA-1

cmds.n: Works today, and hashes become 64 characters. Adopt with caution: SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories cannot push to each other, and major hosts still speak SHA-1. For ordinary threat models, hardened SHA-1 already detects known collision attacks.

variants.undo: There is no in-place conversion back; re-init and re-import

intents.q: GitHub App or OAuth app for my integration

cmds.n: Installed per repository with fine-grained permissions, acting as itself with short-lived tokens. This is what GitHub recommends for almost everything new.
You genuinely need to act as the user across everything they can reach, like a sign-in-with-GitHub flow.

intents.q: Stop changelog files from conflicting

cmds.n: Merges keep both sides' added lines instead of conflicting. Only for append-mostly files: union never reports conflicts, and line order between sides is not guaranteed.

intents.q: Diff binary documents as text

cmds.n: Pair with git config diff.pandoc.textconv "pandoc --to=markdown": diffs convert the document to text first, so changes read as prose. exiftool does the same for image metadata.

intents.q: Which hook fires when

cmds.n: Before the commit is recorded: linting and formatting. commit-msg validates the message.
Before anything leaves: the last cheap gate for tests.
After a pull lands: the classic spot to reinstall dependencies when the lockfile changed. post-checkout fires on branch switches.

variants.undo: Hooks live in .git/hooks or core.hooksPath; delete the file

intents.q: Get every page from the GitHub API

cmds.n: Follows the Link headers until the list ends; without it you silently get the first 30. Add per_page=100 to cut round trips.

intents.q: GitLab CI and GitHub Actions, translated

cmds.n: GitLab's stages map to job needs: chains; script lines map to run steps; include maps to reusable workflows; GitLab runners to self-hosted runners. The concepts translate one-to-one more than either vendor admits.

intents.q: Structure an organization with teams

cmds.n: Grant repositories to teams, never to individuals: joining a team grants everything at once. Teams nest, so platform/backend inherits from platform, and @org/team mentions and CODEOWNERS entries come free.

variants.undo: Delete the team; repository access via other paths survives

intents.q: Token works everywhere except my company org
aka: ssh key not authorized for org

cmds.c: Settings -> Developer settings -> Tokens -> Configure SSO -> Authorize
cmds.n: SAML-protected organizations require each token and SSH key to be authorized for them explicitly, one click per org. The token itself is fine; it just has not been introduced.

variants.undo: Revoke the authorization in the same menu

intents.q: SSH, GPG, or gitsign for signing commits

cmds.n: Reuses the key you already push with; two config lines and the Verified badge appears. The right answer for individuals.
GPG remains for ecosystems built on its web of trust, like kernel work. Sigstore's gitsign signs keylessly against your OIDC identity, aimed at supply-chain verification in organizations.

intents.q: Export a software bill of materials

cmds.n: SPDX JSON of everything the dependency graph sees, the artifact compliance reviews ask for. Scriptable at /dependency-graph/sbom via gh api.

intents.q: Deploy to a cloud with no stored keys

cmds.n: The workflow requests a short-lived identity token; the cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP) is configured to trust this repository's workflows and issues temporary credentials. Nothing long-lived exists to leak or rotate.
With role-to-assume: the official actions handle the exchange.

variants.undo: Remove the trust relationship in the cloud account

intents.q: Use gh inside a workflow

cmds.n: gh is preinstalled on GitHub runners and authenticates from that variable alone: no login step. Grant the job the permissions the command needs, like issues: write to comment.

intents.q: Delete old workflow runs

cmds.c: gh run list --status failure --json databaseId -q ".[].databaseId" | xargs -n1 gh run delete
cmds.n: Deletes matching runs, here every failure. Retention eventually removes logs on its own; this is for tidying now. Run it in Git Bash on Windows.

variants.undo: None; runs are gone for good

intents.q: Stop a hung job from burning six hours

cmds.n: On the job or a single step. The default is 360 minutes, which is 360 minutes of billing when something wedges. Set it just above your worst honest run.

intents.q: Rulesets or classic branch protection

cmds.n: Rulesets are the successor: they layer, target patterns of branches and tags, work at organization level, and can run in evaluate mode before enforcing. Classic protection still works; new setups should not start there.

variants.undo: Delete the ruleset; nothing else changes

intents.q: See who changed what in the organization

cmds.n: Searchable events for settings, access, and repository changes: action:repo.destroy or actor:<user> narrow it. Reachable at /orgs/<org>/audit-log via gh api for retention beyond the UI window.

intents.q: Sign commits with no key to manage

cmds.n: Signing rides your OIDC login through Sigstore instead of a key file: nothing to back up, nothing to leak, a transparency log entry per signature. Verification tooling is still maturing outside supply-chain contexts; individuals are usually better served by SSH signing.

intents.q: Move a repository to GitHub from another host

cmds.n: A complete copy: branches, tags, notes.
Everything lands in the new empty repository. Then update remotes in every working clone.

variants.undo: Delete the new repository; the source is untouched

cmds.n: GitHub's importer handles Subversion, Mercurial, and plain Git URLs. Issue history from GitLab or Jira needs a dedicated migration tool or the API.

intents.q: Work with Azure DevOps Repos

cmds.n: Ordinary Git underneath: branches, tags, and hooks all behave. Pull requests there mean the same thing they do on GitHub.
The Azure CLI covers what gh covers on GitHub.

intents.q: Bitbucket Pipelines next to GitHub Actions

cmds.n: One file at the root, steps built from Docker images, secrets as repository variables. Actions' marketplace of reusable steps is the main thing without a direct equal; Pipes are the nearest idea.

intents.q: Speed up log and blame on a big repository

cmds.n: Precomputes the commit walk. log --graph, blame, and merge-base get dramatically faster on large histories.
Keeps it fresh automatically, along with other upkeep.

intents.q: Make git status instant on huge working trees

cmds.n: A built-in file-system monitor tells Git what changed instead of Git scanning every path. Pair with git config core.untrackedCache true. The difference on a monorepo is seconds to milliseconds.

intents.q: When aggressive repacking is worth it

cmds.n: Rarely needed: normal gc is enough, and aggressive runs cost hours on big repos. Worth one run after a history rewrite or an import that left the object store messy.

variants.undo: Nothing to undo; repacking never changes history

intents.q: Keep only some folders in the history

cmds.n: Rewrites every commit to contain only those paths, dropping commits that touched nothing else. --invert-paths removes them instead. Every hash changes, so this is for fresh copies, never a shared repository.

variants.undo: None in place; work on a clone and keep the original

intents.q: Graft old history onto a truncated repository

cmds.n: Joins a truncated history to an archived one without rewriting anything: log and blame follow through the join. The replacement is local until pushed with git push origin refs/replace/*.

intents.q: Diff the very first commit

cmds.n: The root commit has no parent, so plain diffs come out empty. --root shows it as all additions.
That constant is the empty tree, useful in scripts that must diff anything against nothing.

intents.q: Target files precisely with pathspecs
aka: git add all but one file

cmds.n: The :(exclude) prefix subtracts from a match. Quote it so the shell leaves it alone.
:(top) anchors at the root no matter where you stand; :(icase) matches case-insensitively.

intents.q: Stash without touching the working tree

cmds.n: Builds a stash commit and prints its hash, changing nothing on disk. The scriptable way to snapshot a dirty tree before a risky operation.
Files that commit into the stash list so it survives garbage collection.

intents.q: Is git gc ever going to delete my work

cmds.n: Safe by design: anything reachable from a branch, tag, stash, index, or reflog is kept. Loose unreachable objects survive a two-week grace period, and reflog entries ninety days. Only gc --prune=now removes them immediately, which is why panic-recovery advice always says stop running that.

intents.q: Deploy to Heroku with Git

cmds.n: Adds a remote named heroku to this folder. From then on git push heroku main deploys.
Heroku authenticates the push by SSH key or by the CLI's HTTP credentials. This uploads the key that publickey errors are complaining about.

intents.q: Unlink of file failed on Windows
aka: unlink of file failed should i try again

cmds.n: Something has the file open: a dev server, an editor indexing, antivirus, or Explorer previewing. Close it and answer yes to retry.
On for Git for Windows by default; confirm it is not disabled. Excluding the working folder from real-time antivirus scanning cures the stubborn cases.

intents.q: Remove a folder from the remote but keep it locally
aka: delete folder from github not disk

cmds.n: Ignore it first, or the next add puts it straight back.

cmds.c: git rm -r --cached build/ && git commit -m "Stop tracking build output" && git push
cmds.n: Gone from the repository and from GitHub, still on your disk. Teammates lose their copy on pull, which is usually the point.

variants.undo: git revert the commit restores tracking

intents.q: Reset a remote branch to an older commit
aka: resetting remote to a certain commit

cmds.n: Move your local branch first.
The remote follows. Anyone who already pulled keeps the newer commits and will try to push them back, so tell the team before, not after.

variants.undo: git reflog for the old tip, then force-push it back

cmds.n: Undoes the same changes by adding new commits. Nobody's clone breaks, and the record stays honest.

intents.q: Should .gitignore be committed

cmds.n: Commit it: the rules are part of the project and every clone needs them. It shows as untracked only because you have not yet.
Same syntax, never committed, invisible to everyone else. The right home for personal ignores.

intents.q: Git opened an editor asking why this merge is necessary
aka: please enter a commit message to explain why this merge

cmds.n: In Vim, or Ctrl+X in nano. The prefilled message is fine; the prompt only wants you to confirm it. Nothing has gone wrong.

Rebasing on pull produces no merge commit, so nothing to describe. To keep merging but skip the prompt: git config --global merge.ff true accepts fast-forwards silently, and pull --no-edit takes the default message.

intents.q: Clone using a username and password or token

cmds.n: Passwords have not worked for Git operations on GitHub since 2021; use a token. It lands in your shell history and in .git/config, so prefer a credential helper for daily work and this only for one-shot scripts.
Fails fast instead of hanging on a prompt no one can answer: what CI wants.

intents.q: Update branches without checking them out

cmds.n: Fast-forwards local main while you stay where you are. It refuses anything that is not a fast-forward, so it cannot mangle work.
Updates every remote-tracking branch. Local branches stay put, which is precisely what makes it safe to run any time.

intents.q: Resolve conflicts in the VS Code merge editor

cmds.n: The button on a conflicted file. Three panes: your side, theirs, and the result you are building. Accept either, accept both, or edit the result directly, then Complete Merge stages it.
Adds the common ancestor between the two sides, so you can see what each side changed rather than guessing.

intents.q: Read conflict markers properly

cmds.n: Everything to the divider is your side. Below it, to the closing marker, is the incoming side, labelled with its branch or commit.
Adds a third section showing the common ancestor. Knowing what both sides started from turns most guesswork into a decision.

intents.q: During a rebase, ours and theirs are swapped
aka: which side is mine in rebase

cmds.n: In a rebase, ours is the branch you are replaying onto, and theirs is your own commit being replayed. Backwards from a merge, because Git is applying your work as a patch onto their base.
When in doubt, read the header: it names the commit currently being applied.

intents.q: Cherry-pick or merge for one fix from another branch
aka: take one commit or the whole branch

cmds.n: Copies the change as a new commit with a new hash. Fine for a hotfix that must land on two branches, but if the source branch merges later, the same change exists twice in history.
Brings everything and records the relationship, so nothing is ever applied twice. Prefer merging unless you truly need one commit early.

variants.undo: git revert the cherry-pick, or reset before pushing

intents.q: Can two commits have the same hash

cmds.n: Full hashes are 160 bits; accidental collision is not a risk anyone has to plan for, and Git ships collision detection against the known SHA-1 attack.
Seven characters do collide in big repositories, and Git errors with ambiguous argument. It lengthens abbreviations automatically as a repo grows; this sets a floor.

intents.q: Signing fails with gpg failed to sign the data
aka: gpg failed to sign the data

cmds.n: Reproduces the failure outside Git. A passphrase prompt that never appears is the usual cause.
Add it to your shell profile so the agent knows where to prompt. On Windows, confirming user.signingkey matches a key gpg --list-secret-keys shows fixes most of the rest.

variants.undo: git config --global commit.gpgsign false while you debug

intents.q: Fix a repository with mixed line endings

cmds.n: Declares the policy in the repository, where it belongs, instead of relying on each developer's config.

cmds.c: git add --renormalize . && git commit -m "Normalize line endings"
cmds.n: One commit that touches every affected file. Merge open branches first: this diff conflicts with everything.

intents.q: CI commit fails: please tell me who you are

cmds.n: Runners have no identity of their own.
That address is the official Actions bot, so commits show its avatar rather than a broken one.

intents.q: GitHub says the diff is too large to display

cmds.n: The web view hides individual files past a size threshold and stops rendering entirely on very large pull requests. The terminal has no such limit.

cmds.c: gh pr checkout <number> && git diff main...HEAD -- <path>
cmds.n: Read it file by file locally. A diff too big to render is usually also too big to review well: splitting it is the real fix.

intents.q: Submodule is always in detached HEAD

cmds.n: A submodule is pinned to an exact commit, not a branch, so checking one out lands on that commit with no branch attached. That is correct behavior, not a fault.
Attach to a branch first, commit and push from inside the submodule, then commit the new pointer in the parent repository.

intents.q: Git will not track my empty folder

cmds.n: Git records files, not folders, so an empty one cannot exist in a commit. A placeholder file creates the folder on clone. .gitkeep is convention, not a Git feature: any filename works.

intents.q: Should this be a branch or a tag

cmds.n: A tag is a permanent marker on one commit: use it for anything you want to point back to forever.
A branch moves as work continues: use it when patches will keep landing on that line. Releases usually need both, a branch to maintain and a tag per shipped version.

intents.q: Link GitHub work to Jira

cmds.c: git commit -m "PROJ-482 Fix timeout on retry"
cmds.n: With the GitHub for Jira app installed, the issue key anywhere in a commit message, branch name, or pull request title links the work automatically and shows the development panel in Jira.

variants.undo: Remove the app from the organization

intents.q: Get repository activity in Slack

cmds.n: After /github signin. Pick the event types deliberately: subscribing to everything trains the channel to ignore it.

intents.q: Dependency updates beyond Dependabot

cmds.n: Renovate groups related upgrades into one pull request, schedules them, and can auto-merge low-risk ones. More configuration than Dependabot, correspondingly more control on repositories with many dependencies.

variants.undo: Remove the app and the config file

intents.q: Manage hooks with the pre-commit framework

cmds.n: Declares hooks by repository and version, so the whole team runs identical checks. Hooks themselves are not versioned by Git, which is the gap this fills.
Writes the actual Git hook. pre-commit run --all-files checks the existing codebase once.

intents.q: Enforce a commit message convention

cmds.n: From a commit-msg hook: messages that break the convention are refused before the commit exists.

cmds.c: Ruleset -> Require merge queue or a status check
cmds.n: Local hooks can be skipped, so enforce in CI too: a check that lints the pull request title is enough when you squash-merge.

intents.q: Version and publish automatically from commit messages

cmds.n: Reads Conventional Commits since the last tag, decides major, minor, or patch, writes the changelog, tags, and publishes. release-please does the same through a release pull request you approve.

variants.undo: Delete the tag and release; unpublish per registry rules

intents.q: Version a monorepo's packages independently

cmds.n: Each pull request adds a small markdown file describing its change and impact. The release job consumes them all, bumps only the packages affected, and writes per-package changelogs.

variants.undo: Delete the changeset files before release

intents.q: Build only what changed in a monorepo

cmds.n: Compares against the base to build only touched packages and their dependents. Nx calls it nx affected. Both need full history, so set fetch-depth: 0 on checkout.

variants.undo: Drop the filter to build everything

intents.q: Move files already in history into LFS
aka: repo huge because of old binaries

cmds.n: Rewrites history so those files become LFS pointers, which is the only way to shrink a repository that is already large. Every hash changes: coordinate with the team, then force-push, and have everyone reclone.

variants.undo: git lfs migrate export --include="*.psd" reverses it, with another rewrite

intents.q: Review pull requests inside VS Code

cmds.n: Lists pull requests and issues in the sidebar, checks one out with a click, and shows review comments inline against the code. Approving and commenting happen without leaving the editor.

intents.q: Put my first project on GitHub, start to finish

cmds.c: git init && git add . && git commit -m "First commit"
cmds.n: History begins locally. Check nothing secret is included before this line.
Creates the repository, wires it up, and pushes. Without gh: create it empty on the site, then git remote add origin <url> and git push -u origin main.

variants.undo: gh repo delete <name>, and remove .git to undo the local history

intents.q: The four commands most days need
aka: what do i run each day

cmds.n: Start from what everyone else has done.
Stage deliberately, reviewing each change as it goes in.
Record it, small enough to describe in a line.
Publish. Everything else in Git exists for the days this loop is not enough.

variants.undo: Each step has its own undo; nothing here is irreversible

intents.q: Try something risky without fear

cmds.n: A branch is free and disposable. If the idea fails, delete it and main never knew.
Commit early on the branch: committed work is recoverable through the reflog for months, while uncommitted work is the only kind Git can truly lose.

variants.undo: git switch - and git branch -D try/idea

intents.q: The one mental model that makes Git click

cmds.n: Git is a graph of snapshots plus labels pointing into it. Commits are immutable snapshots chained to their parents; branches, tags, and HEAD are movable labels. Nearly every command either adds a snapshot or moves a label, and knowing which one it does tells you how dangerous it is.

intents.q: Which undo command do I need

cmds.n: Discards edits in the working tree. git restore --staged <file> unstages without discarding.

variants.undo: None once discarded; the file was never recorded

cmds.n: Removes the commit, keeps the work. --hard removes both. Rewriting is fine while the commits are still only yours.

variants.undo: git reset --soft HEAD@{1} through the reflog

cmds.n: A new commit that cancels the old one. Nobody's clone breaks, and the record stays honest.

intents.q: Read a Git error message properly

cmds.n: Git's errors almost always end with the fix: hint lines suggest the exact command, and status states what is in progress. Read the last three lines first, then run status before trying anything from the internet.

intents.q: When Git is the wrong tool
aka: should i use git for this

cmds.n: Secrets, credentials, and personal data: never. Generated output and dependencies: no, they belong to a build. Huge binaries that change often: only through LFS or object storage. Live databases and user uploads: not at all. Git versions source, not state.

intents.q: I think I lost work: the recovery order

cmds.n: First: it may simply be on another branch or still staged.
Second: shelved work hides here and survives branch switches.
Third, and usually the answer: every position HEAD has held for about ninety days, including commits no branch points to.
Last: objects nothing references at all. Stop running gc --prune until you are done looking.

variants.undo: Recovery only adds references; nothing here destroys anything

intents.q: Git refused to do what I asked

cmds.n: Refusal is a feature: Git stops when a command would silently lose work you cannot get back. Uncommitted changes in the way, a non-fast-forward push, deleting an unmerged branch. Commit or stash, then retry.
The capital or forced version of a command overrides the guard: -D, --force, --hard. Reach for these knowing exactly what the guard was protecting.

variants.undo: git reflog, while the entries last

intents.q: The Git words everyone assumes you know

cmds.n: HEAD is where you stand. A ref is any name pointing at a commit, so branches and tags are refs. The index is the staging area. A tree is a folder snapshot, a blob is file content.
origin is the default remote's nickname; upstream is either the original repository you forked or the remote branch yours tracks. Tracking is the link that lets push and pull work bare.

intents.q: Use Git with a Unity project

cmds.n: Library, Temp, and Build stay out; .meta files must always be committed, or Unity loses every asset reference.
Art assets belong in LFS from the first commit, not after the repository is already heavy.

cmds.c: Editor -> Project Settings -> Asset Serialization -> Force Text
cmds.n: Text serialization at least makes conflicts readable. Unity's Smart Merge tool, wired as a mergetool, resolves most of them.

intents.q: Stop Jupyter notebooks from polluting diffs

cmds.n: Installs a filter that strips outputs and execution counts on commit, so diffs show code changes only. Your local notebook keeps its outputs.
nbdiff renders notebook diffs cell by cell instead of as JSON noise.

intents.q: Never commit Terraform state

cmds.n: State files hold secrets in plain text and cannot merge; two people applying from Git-tracked state corrupt each other's infrastructure.
A remote backend with locking is the answer state needs. Git versions the configuration; the backend versions the state.

intents.q: Version a WordPress site sensibly

cmds.n: Version what you write: your theme and custom plugins. Core, uploads, and the database do not belong in Git; core is a dependency and the database is live state.

intents.q: Git settings for an Android or Gradle project

cmds.n: Keeps build, .gradle, and local.properties out; the last holds machine-specific SDK paths that break everyone else's build.
Commit the wrapper: it pins the Gradle version so every machine and CI runner builds identically.

intents.q: Git settings for a .NET or Visual Studio project

cmds.n: Writes the official .NET ignore file: bin, obj, .vs, and user-specific .suo and .user files stay out.
Solution files conflict constantly on projects added in parallel; union merging removes most of that friction.

intents.q: Version design files with the code

cmds.n: Binary design sources belong in LFS: versioned, but not bloating every clone. They cannot merge, so agree who owns a file before editing.

cmds.c: Export to SVG for anything reviewed
cmds.n: SVG and other text formats diff and render in pull requests, which is what makes design review possible in the repository at all. Figma and similar tools keep their own history; link to it rather than mirroring it.

intents.q: Run documentation like code

cmds.n: Markdown in docs/, reviewed through pull requests alongside the code that changed. MkDocs, Docusaurus, and Sphinx all build from it.
A workflow builds and deploys on every merge, so published documentation can never drift from main.

intents.q: Structure a data science repository

cmds.n: Code, notebooks, and configuration in Git. Data and model weights out, tracked by DVC or object storage with a pointer committed.
Keeps notebook diffs reviewable. Pin dependencies in a lockfile so a result from six months ago can be reproduced at all.

intents.q: Use Git for a group assignment

cmds.n: Private, one repository, everyone as a collaborator. Add each member so contributions are attributed individually, which matters when marks are.
One branch per person or section, merged through pull requests. It costs an hour to learn and saves the night before the deadline.

intents.q: soft, mixed, and hard reset compared
aka: reset soft vs mixed vs hard

cmds.n: Moves the branch only. Staging area and files untouched, so the changes sit staged and ready to recommit.
The default. Moves the branch and clears the staging area; your files keep every change, unstaged.
Moves the branch and overwrites your files. The only one that destroys work, and the only one worth hesitating over.

variants.undo: git reset --hard HEAD@{1} restores the position; uncommitted work lost to --hard is gone

intents.q: Why checkout does three unrelated things

cmds.n: One command grew to switch branches, restore files, and detach HEAD, which is why its behavior seemed to depend on mood. Git 2.23 split it deliberately.
Branches only, and it refuses ambiguous arguments.
Files only. Same power, no chance of restoring a file when you meant to change branch.

variants.undo: Each has its own undo; checkout still works for old habits

intents.q: Merge strategies and when they matter

cmds.n: Modern Git uses ort, which replaced recursive: faster, better at renames, same behavior you already expect. You rarely need to name a strategy.

variants.undo: git merge --abort or git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD

cmds.n: Resolves only conflicting hunks in their favor, keeping everything non-conflicting from both. Different from -s ours, which discards the other side's changes entirely while still recording the merge.

intents.q: Diff a pull request the way GitHub does

cmds.n: Three dots measures from the common ancestor, so changes that landed on main meanwhile do not pollute the diff. This is exactly what the Files changed tab shows.
The changed-file list for linting only what the branch touched. Requires full history: set fetch-depth 0 on checkout.

intents.q: Rebase or pull without stashing first

cmds.n: Git shelves your uncommitted work, rebases, and puts it back. Removes the most common reason a pull stops with an error.
If reapplying conflicts, the work stays safely in the stash rather than vanishing. Check here whenever an autostashed rebase ends noisily.

variants.undo: git stash pop when the tree is ready

intents.q: Review a pull request without disturbing your work

cmds.n: A second folder on another branch, sharing one repository and object store. Your main folder keeps its dirty tree, running server, and build cache untouched.
Clean up when done. worktree list shows what exists.

variants.undo: git worktree remove, or prune if the folder was deleted by hand

intents.q: Find the commit that broke it, fast

cmds.c: git bisect start && git bisect bad && git bisect good <old-hash>
cmds.n: Git checks out the midpoint; mark each as good or bad and it halves the range. Ten steps cover a thousand commits.
Returns to where you started, whatever happened.
Any script exiting zero for good and non-zero for bad. Walk away; Git names the culprit commit itself.

intents.q: Make Git remember conflict resolutions

cmds.n: Git records how you resolved each conflict and replays it automatically the next time the identical conflict appears. On a long-lived branch rebased repeatedly, this is the difference between painful and routine.
What it is currently tracking. Resolutions live in .git/rr-cache, local to your machine.

variants.undo: git rerere forget <path> discards a bad recorded resolution

intents.q: A quarterly checkup for a repository

cmds.c: git fetch --prune && git branch -vv | grep ": gone]"
cmds.n: Clear branches whose remotes are gone.
Watch the size trend; investigate before it becomes a rewrite.
Open security alerts, plus a glance at stale pull requests and untriaged issues. Twenty minutes a quarter keeps a repository from decaying into an archaeology project.

intents.q: Set a different identity per folder

cmds.n: In ~/.gitconfig. Every repository under ~/work automatically uses the work identity, signing key, and remotes. No more commits authored by the wrong person.
Run inside a repository to confirm which identity actually applies.

intents.q: Run a step only sometimes

cmds.n: On a step or a job. Expressions read the event context, so branch, actor, and event type are all available.
By default a failed step cancels the rest; always() runs cleanup regardless, and failure() runs only when something broke.

intents.q: Never paste untrusted input into a run block

cmds.n: Expressions are substituted as text before the shell runs, so a title containing shell syntax executes on your runner. Titles, branch names, and issue bodies are all attacker-controlled.
Pass through an environment variable and reference "$TITLE" in the script. The shell then treats it as data, never as code.

intents.q: Pin third-party actions safely

cmds.n: A tag can be moved by its owner; a full commit SHA cannot. Pinning by SHA means the code you reviewed is the code that runs.
Restrict which actions may run at all. Dependabot updates SHA pins for you, so pinning does not mean freezing forever.

variants.undo: Loosen the policy or repoint the pin

intents.q: Prove a build artifact came from your repository

cmds.n: Signs a statement binding the artifact to the exact workflow, commit, and repository, backed by Sigstore. The job needs id-token: write and attestations: write.
Anyone can check a downloaded binary against that claim.

variants.undo: Attestations cannot be unpublished; issue a new release

intents.q: Publish packages to GitHub Packages

cmds.n: Scoped to your org, authenticated with a token or the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN. npm, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems, and containers are all supported.
The permission a workflow needs to publish. Package visibility follows the repository it is linked to.

variants.undo: Delete the package version under Packages

intents.q: Tame the GitHub notification inbox

cmds.n: An inbox, not a feed: filter with is:unread reason:mention, then Done to archive. reason: values like review-requested, author, and team-mention separate what needs you from what merely happened.

variants.undo: Undone items return from the Done view

intents.q: What GitHub Pages will and will not do

cmds.n: Static files only: no server-side code, no databases. Soft limits of 1 GB per site, 100 GB bandwidth a month, and ten builds an hour. HTTPS is automatic, including on custom domains.
Keep the static site on Pages and call an API elsewhere, or move the whole site to a platform with functions.

intents.q: Publish a Pages site only my team can see

cmds.n: Available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud: visitors must be signed in with repository access. On other plans a Pages site from a private repository is still published publicly, which surprises people badly.

intents.q: Make gh fit your habits

cmds.n: Used whenever gh opens an editor. gh config set git_protocol ssh makes every clone use SSH.
Aliases for the commands you type daily; they accept arguments and shell expansion.

variants.undo: gh alias delete prs, or set the config back

intents.q: Read a repository's Insights honestly

cmds.n: Commit counts and code frequency show rhythm, not merit: a refactor moves thousands of lines, a critical fix moves one. Read Traffic and Community for adoption and health, Dependency graph for risk.

intents.q: Undo edits to one file without touching the rest
aka: undo changes in one file only

cmds.n: Rewrites the file from the last commit. The edits are not in Git, so they are gone.

variants.undo: None, unless your editor's local history has it

cmds.n: Clears it from the staging area and the working tree in one move.

intents.q: Read a file on the remote without pulling

cmds.n: Downloads the remote state without touching your branch or files.
Prints their version. Diff it against yours with git diff HEAD origin/main -- <path>.

intents.q: Find out who is allowed to merge my pull request

cmds.n: Shows who was asked and where the decision stands.
Path patterns decide who is requested automatically, and rulesets can make their approval mandatory.

intents.q: Start a branch with no files at all

cmds.n: A branch with no parent commit. Your files carry over staged, so clear them if you want a true blank start.
Empties the tree. Common for a docs-only or gh-pages branch that shares no history with the code.

variants.undo: git switch - returns; delete the orphan with git branch -D

intents.q: Work on a tag without the detached-HEAD warning

cmds.n: Tags are read-only points, so commits need a branch. Creating one from the tag is the whole answer.

variants.undo: git switch - and delete the branch

intents.q: Count how many files a change touches

cmds.n: Files changed, insertions, deletions, one line.
Just the count, for scripts and pull-request size checks.

intents.q: Restore an entire folder from another commit

cmds.n: Every file under that path returns to how the commit had it. Deletions inside the folder are restored too.
Review before committing; this can be a large change.

intents.q: Find out who deleted a branch and when

cmds.c: gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/events --jq '.[] | select(.type=="DeleteEvent") | {who: .actor.login, ref: .payload.ref, when: .created_at}'
cmds.n: Recent deletions with the actor. Organizations keep this far longer in the audit log.
Your own machine's record of when it went, and the hash to restore it from.

intents.q: Clone with only the last few months of history

cmds.n: Everything newer, nothing older. Better than --depth when you care about a time window rather than a commit count.

intents.q: See exactly what a pull would change before running it

cmds.n: Nothing in your working tree moves.
The full shape of what is coming. git log HEAD..origin/main lists the commits behind it.

intents.q: A contributor's pull request contains a secret

cmds.n: Assume it is compromised the moment it was pushed anywhere public. Everything else is secondary.
Close rather than merge, and ask for a fresh branch. Merging then reverting leaves the secret in history forever.

variants.undo: Nothing to undo; rotation is the fix

intents.q: See who owns each branch and how stale it is

cmds.n: Every remote branch, newest first, with its last author. The cleanup list writes itself.

intents.q: I ran git add on everything by mistake

cmds.n: Everything returns to unstaged. Your edits are untouched: only the staging area changes.
Or unstage selectively and keep the rest ready to commit.

intents.q: Keep a repository on GitHub and another host at once

variants.when: Push to both with one command

cmds.n: Adds a second push destination to origin. Repeat for the first URL, since adding one replaces the default.
Confirms both push lines are present before you rely on it.

intents.q: Find which files bloated the repository
aka: what is making my repo large

cmds.c: git rev-list --objects --all --missing=allow-any | git cat-file --batch-check="%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)" | awk '$1=="blob"' | sort -k3 -n -r | head -20
cmds.n: The twenty largest blobs ever committed, with their paths. Run it in Git Bash on Windows.
The total, so you know whether the top offenders explain the size.

intents.q: My commit shows Verified on GitHub but not locally
aka: verified badge but local says no signature

cmds.n: GitHub checks against keys registered on the author's account. Your machine checks against your own allowed-signers file, which is usually empty.
Add the signer lines you trust and local verification starts matching.

intents.q: Open a pull request from my fork to the original

cmds.n: Push to your fork, which is the only place you can write.
Names the upstream repository as the target and your fork branch as the source.

intents.q: Commit some lines of a file and leave the rest

cmds.n: Walks the file hunk by hunk: y to stage, n to skip, s to split smaller, e to edit the hunk by hand.
Confirm exactly what the commit will contain before making it.

intents.q: Fix a wrong email across many commits

cmds.n: Rewrites each commit with your current identity. Set user.email correctly first.

cmds.c: Add the old address to your GitHub account
cmds.n: Under Settings -> Emails. The commits link to you retroactively with no rewriting, which is almost always the better trade.

intents.q: Stop tracking a folder that should never have been committed

cmds.n: Ignore it first, or it comes straight back.

cmds.c: git rm -r --cached node_modules && git commit -m "Stop tracking build output"
cmds.n: Removes it from the repository going forward; the folder stays on disk. History still holds the old copies, which only a rewrite removes.

variants.undo: git revert the commit re-adds the tracking

intents.q: Cherry-pick or rebase to move work

cmds.n: Copies chosen commits and leaves the originals where they are, so the change exists twice. Right for backporting one fix.

variants.when: A whole branch onto a new base

cmds.n: Moves every commit of the branch, rewriting them once. Right for keeping a feature current.

intents.q: Throw away local commits and take the remote exactly
aka: discard local commits and take remote

cmds.n: Get their state first.
Your branch becomes theirs. Local commits not pushed anywhere are lost to everything except the reflog.
Only if you also want untracked files gone; this part has no undo.

variants.undo: git reset --hard HEAD@{1} for the commits; nothing for cleaned files

intents.q: Rename a file to different capitalisation

cmds.n: On Windows and macOS the filesystem sees both names as the same file, so Git needs telling explicitly.
Only for repositories that must stay case-exact; it can surface confusing duplicates otherwise.

intents.q: List what shipped in a release

cmds.n: Exactly what the release added.
Every release that includes that commit, which answers the support question directly.

intents.q: When to use gh instead of git

cmds.n: git moves commits, branches, and history: everything that exists in the repository itself.
gh drives the things that exist only on GitHub: pull requests, issues, releases, workflows, and the API. Neither replaces the other.

intents.q: Work privately on a public project

cmds.n: Forks of public repositories are always public, so mirror instead of forking.
Push into a private repository you created empty. Pull upstream updates by adding it as a second remote.

intents.q: Delete a branch on the server but keep mine
aka: remove branch from github not locally

cmds.n: Removes it from the remote. Your local branch and its commits stay untouched.
Optional, so Git stops reporting the branch as gone.

variants.undo: git push -u origin <branch> puts it back

intents.q: Find when a commit or file version was made

cmds.n: Date, author, and subject in one line.
When that file was last touched, which the filesystem timestamp cannot tell you after a clone.

intents.q: Share one computer between two Git identities

cmds.n: Local config beats global, so each clone can carry its own identity.
Both people get credit on the same commit without switching anything.

intents.q: Protect main when I am the only maintainer

cmds.n: Require a pull request and leave the bypass list empty so the rule binds you too. Free on public repositories.

cmds.c:
printf '#!/bin/sh
[ "$(git branch --show-current)" = main ] && echo "Use a branch" && exit 1
exit 0
' > .git/hooks/pre-commit
cmds.n: A hook that stops the habit before it starts. Make it executable with chmod +x.

intents.q: Download only one folder of a repository

cmds.n: Downloads almost nothing up front.
Only that path appears on disk; commits and pulls still work normally.
Or download the ZIP from the site when history is irrelevant.

intents.q: The clone is far larger than the files

cmds.n: History holds every version ever committed, so a repository with churned binaries dwarfs its checkout.
Skips old file contents until needed, which fixes the symptom without rewriting anything.

intents.q: Clean up my branch before asking for review

cmds.n: Fold the wip commits into meaningful ones, reword messages, drop dead ends. Safe while the branch is yours alone.
Updates the branch and refuses if someone else pushed meanwhile.

variants.undo: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD, then force-push again

intents.q: Know what Git does automatically behind my back
aka: does git run on its own

cmds.n: Git repacks loose objects opportunistically after some commands. That is the only routine background work in a default install.
Scheduled upkeep is opt-in, not default. Nothing phones home, and nothing pushes on your behalf.

intents.q: Undo a rename before committing

cmds.n: Renaming back is the cleanest undo; Git records the net effect as nothing.
Or reset both paths to the last commit if you also edited the contents.

intents.q: Get my GitHub notifications under control

cmds.n: The inbox has filters: is:unread reason:mention cuts to what actually needs you. Done clears an item; Unsubscribe stops the thread.
Send most things to the web inbox and keep email for mentions and reviews only.

intents.q: Check a downloaded release is genuine

cmds.n: Confirms the file is the one the maintainer built, provided the checksum file itself came from the release page.
Proves the artifact was built by that repository's workflow, which a checksum alone cannot.
